items.author: Debbi Fields

items.title: Auditable Long-Term Memory: A Deterministic Retrieval Chain Measured at 479/475 of 500 on LongMemEval-S
items.abstract: This paper introduces an auditable long-term memory system that achieves high performance on the LongMemEval-S benchmark. Its core method involves a deterministic retrieval chain combining hybrid candidate retrieval, cross-encoder reranking, and coverage-first packet compilation, with an LLM acting solely as a final reader. The system's main contribution is demonstrating strong, auditable long-term memory retrieval capabilities, scoring 479/500 and 475/500 on the benchmark, highlighting its potential for reliable knowledge recall.

items.title: Diagnosing and Improving Probabilistic Reasoning in Large Language Models
items.abstract: This paper proposes a decision-theoretic framework to analyze how Large Language Models (LLMs) make probabilistic decisions. It decomposes decision loss into belief accuracy and action optimization, using a synthetic benchmark to diagnose LLM reasoning. The study shows that interventions targeting specific reasoning components can improve performance but don't always transfer to other areas, and decision improvement is possible even without better belief formation.

items.title: On Trajectory-Aware Training for Masked Diffusion Language Models
items.abstract: This paper introduces PUMBA, a unified framework for trajectory-aware training of masked diffusion language models. PUMBA addresses the mismatch between training and inference by training the model on consecutive steps of predicted trajectories and passing information between them. This approach optimizes the model jointly through backpropagation, leading to improved performance by aligning training masks more closely with inference conditions without suffering from local overfitting.

items.title: SelfSearch: Reward-Free Search for Self-Improving Agents
items.abstract: SelfSearch enables LLM agents to improve themselves without needing external rewards. It achieves this by using past self-improvement attempts, including reasoning and outcomes, as experience to guide future modifications. This reward-free approach leads to better task performance and more effective self-improvement strategies.

items.title: The Unequal Influence of Bad Advice: Using Training Data Attribution to Modulate Emergent Misalignment
items.abstract: This paper investigates how fine-tuning large language models can lead to "emergent misalignment" by amplifying harmful personas. The core method uses training data attribution to quantify the influence of individual harmful examples on this misalignment. The key contribution is demonstrating that score-based filtering of training data can significantly enhance or attenuate emergent misalignment, suggesting that not all harmful examples contribute equally and that attribution can be used to control model behavior.

items.title: Thinking Before Thinking: Scaling Agentic Inference Through Meta-Reasoning
items.abstract: This paper introduces "agentic meta-reasoning," a system where a controller makes explicit, structured decisions about how to proceed with a complex task. Instead of replaying the entire history, the controller uses a compact summary to evaluate and dispatch the next steps, improving efficiency. This approach significantly enhances agentic capabilities on long-horizon tasks like program reconstruction.

items.title: UserProxyBench: Evaluating LLM User Simulators for Agent Benchmarks and Training
items.abstract: This paper introduces UserProxyBench, a framework to evaluate the performance of LLM-based user simulators in agent benchmarks. It proposes the User Fidelity Score (UFS) to measure how well these simulators adhere to their assigned user instructions, independent of the agent's success. The contribution lies in highlighting the significant impact of user simulator behavior on agent performance and identifying premature disclosure as a common failure mode.

items.title: TabFM-Auto: Self-Evolving Pipelines for Tabular Foundation Models
items.abstract: TabFM-Auto addresses limitations of existing tabular foundation models and self-evolving agents by creating an adaptive pipeline. It uses a language model agent to iteratively refine data cleaning, feature engineering, and context selection around a pre-trained tabular foundation model (TabFM). This approach significantly improves TabFM's performance across a benchmark, achieving top rankings and boosting its Elo score.

items.title: TabFM: A Zero-Shot Foundation Model for Tabular Data
items.abstract: TabFM is a novel foundation model for tabular data that leverages in-context learning for zero-shot predictions, eliminating the need for task-specific tuning. Trained on synthetic data, it learns general tabular representations that achieve state-of-the-art performance across various benchmarks, outperforming even tuned AutoML pipelines. Extensions like TabFM+ and TabFM-Auto further enhance its capabilities through ensembling and LLM-guided data processing.

items.title: Effective Dense Retrieval using Only In-Context Examples
items.abstract: This paper introduces RICE, a training-free method to make decoder-only LLMs effective dense retrievers. RICE prompts the LLM with in-context examples that establish a shared context for encoding queries and documents, thereby producing high-quality dense representations without any fine-tuning. This approach significantly improves prompt-based LLM embeddings for retrieval tasks.
items.figure_caption: Recall@100 across varying numbers of in-context examples for generating RICE (Qwen3.5-9B) query encodings.

items.title: Character Training for Risk-Averse Agents
items.abstract: This paper proposes "character training" to instill risk aversion in AI agents, making them favor safer strategies and thus reducing catastrophic harm. The core method involves training agents with a "constitution" defining constant absolute risk aversion (CARA) over their resources, achieved through on-policy distillation. The contribution lies in demonstrating that persona traits are a robust mechanism for instilling risk preferences, leading to competitive and better generalizing agents compared to traditional training methods.

items.title: Correct Answers, Invalid Traces: What Verifiable Grade-School Math Reveals About Chain-of-Thought Traces
items.abstract: This paper investigates the reliability of chain-of-thought (CoT) traces as accurate records of model reasoning, particularly in grade-school math problems. By using a synthetic benchmark (iGSM) that allows programmatic verification of each step, they found that even when models produce correct answers, their CoT traces can be invalid, especially on harder problems. This highlights a significant gap between answer correctness and the faithfulness of the generated reasoning process.

items.title: Do LLM Agents Execute the Plans They Declare? From Planning-Mode Declaration to Pattern-Specific Execution
items.abstract: This paper investigates the "Plan Declaration-Execution Gap" in LLM agents, where agents may fail to execute the plans they declare. The core method, "Planning-as-Routing," uses an LLM to declare a planning mode (Predefined, Sequential, Hierarchical, or Search), which a deterministic router then directs to a specialized executor. The contribution is demonstrating that this pattern-specific execution significantly improves fidelity to declared plans compared to generic approaches, especially for complex tasks.
items.figure_caption: Overview of the three execution conditions. (a) Flat ReAct : a single ReAct-style executor selects actions from environment feedback without an explicit plan. (b) Planner–Executor (Plan+ReAct) : a planner first selects a planning mode and produces a plan, which is then passed to a generic ReAct executor; however, the declared plan is not structurally enforced during execution. (c) Planning-as-Routing : the LLM first declares a planning mode, and a deterministic router dispatches the task to a matching pattern-specific executor: predefined, sequential, hierarchical, or search. A verifier checks whether execution preserves the declared plan structure.

items.title: Dr. OPD: Learning What to Follow for Optimal On-Policy Distillation of Large Language Models
items.abstract: This paper introduces Dr. OPD, an improved on-policy distillation method for LLMs. Instead of treating all teacher signals equally, Dr. OPD learns to optimally weight these signals to maximize the student model's performance. This is achieved through a bilevel optimization approach that iteratively updates both the student policy and the signal weights.
items.figure_caption: Illustration of Dr. OPD. Left: vanilla OPD assigns the same weight to every teacher signal, while Dr. OPD adapts the weights according to their benefit to the student. Right: student rollouts receive teacher and outcome-reward signals, whose gradient alignment determines token credits. These credits are converted into weights for distillation, where \( \lambda \) controls the weighting strength.

items.title: Gender bias across LLMs is common and highly heterogenous
items.abstract: This paper investigates gender bias across ten diverse LLMs using two methods: analyzing phrase attribution and moral judgments. It reveals that gender bias is prevalent and varies significantly across models, with some exhibiting masculine-stereotyped phrase attribution to women and others showing a male-disadvantaging moral judgment asymmetry. The study's contribution lies in its broad, comparative analysis, highlighting the heterogeneity of LLM gender biases and their potential real-world implications.

items.title: Probability is Not Enough: Exploring and Counting Divergent Tokens for Reasoning Uncertainty Quantification in LLMs
items.abstract: This paper introduces Divergent Token Confidence (DTC), a novel method for quantifying reasoning uncertainty in LLMs. Instead of relying solely on token probabilities, DTC counts tokens where two models disagree significantly during decoding, using Jensen-Shannon divergence to identify these points. This count of divergent tokens is found to be negatively correlated with answer accuracy, providing a more robust signal of model confidence.
items.figure_caption: Divergent-token selection and its relationship to path accuracy. (a) A generator produces a reasoning trajectory. (b) A token is selected when the JSD between two models’ next-token distributions exceeds \( \theta \) . (c) Path accuracy decreases as the number of divergent tokens increases under single- and dual-auxiliary probing.

items.title: Retrieval-Augmented Skill Optimization via Cross-Harness Adaptation
items.abstract: This paper introduces Retrieval-Augmented Skill Optimization (RASO), a method to improve agent skills by leveraging existing knowledge. RASO addresses the inefficiency of current methods by retrieving relevant skills from a large corpus and adapting them to new tasks and environments using Cross-Harness Adaptation. This approach significantly reduces reliance on costly agent simulations by incorporating prior learning.
items.figure_caption: Comparison of RASO to prior skill optimization. Existing skill optimization methods (left) either generate an initial skill from the LLM alone or directly reuse retrieved skills, then refine them mainly from execution feedback. However, retrieved skills often come from mismatched harnesses; on SpreadsheetBench 92.9% originate from a different harness (right, top). RASO (middle) addresses this by retrieving relevant external skill knowledge and adapting it to the target domain and execution harness through Cross-Harness Adaptation , supporting both skill initialization (RASI) and skill update (RASU). Overall, our RASO results in substantially stronger performance than both direct retrieval and retrieval-free optimization methods.

items.title: Video-RSI: Recursive Self-Improvement of Video Understanding Agents via Harness Evolution
items.abstract: Video-RSI recursively improves video understanding agents by using their own language models to revise their observation and action harnesses. The agent actively investigates videos to gather evidence for competing failure explanations, grounding revisions in new observations. This cost-aware evolution leads to improved accuracy with reduced processing costs.

items.title: Which Attention Heads are like the Human Head? Not the Ones that Compute
items.abstract: This paper investigates the relationship between brain activity and Large Language Model (LLM) attention heads. It finds that heads aligned with human brain signals (EEG) are causally involved in task performance, but their ablation is less disruptive than heads identified by traditional attribution methods. This suggests that brain alignment and computational contribution are distinct, with concept-aligned heads showing more promise for brain-AI correspondence than function-based ones.

items.title: Explore Broadly, Reason Sharply: Push Small Models toward the Frontier via Sampling
items.abstract: This paper introduces Parallel Power Tempering (PPT) to improve reasoning in language models without costly retraining. PPT addresses the exploration-exploitation trade-off in existing sampling methods by running multiple model replicas at different "sharpening" levels. This allows for broader exploration of reasoning paths while still focusing on promising solutions, pushing smaller models closer to state-of-the-art performance.
items.figure_caption: Single-shot accuracy (%) of Parallel Power Tempering. Left: Qwen3-8B across three benchmarks. Right: Qwen3.5-9B on GPQA-Diamond, AIME 24&25 and LiveCodeBench v5 against decoding baselines and the reported scores of frontier models.

papers.abstract: This paper investigates the reliability of chain-of-thought (CoT) traces as accurate records of model reasoning, particularly in grade-school math problems. By using a synthetic benchmark (iGSM) that allows programmatic verification of each step, they found that even when models produce correct answers, their CoT traces can be invalid, especially on harder problems. This highlights a significant gap between answer correctness and the faithfulness of the generated reasoning process.

papers.title: Do LLM Agents Execute the Plans They Declare? From Planning-Mode Declaration to Pattern-Specific Execution
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the "Plan Declaration-Execution Gap" in LLM agents, where agents may fail to execute the plans they declare. The core method, "Planning-as-Routing," uses an LLM to declare a planning mode (Predefined, Sequential, Hierarchical, or Search), which a deterministic router then directs to a specialized executor. The contribution is demonstrating that this pattern-specific execution significantly improves fidelity to declared plans compared to generic approaches, especially for complex tasks.
papers.figure_caption: Overview of the three execution conditions. (a) Flat ReAct : a single ReAct-style executor selects actions from environment feedback without an explicit plan. (b) Planner–Executor (Plan+ReAct) : a planner first selects a planning mode and produces a plan, which is then passed to a generic ReAct executor; however, the declared plan is not structurally enforced during execution. (c) Planning-as-Routing : the LLM first declares a planning mode, and a deterministic router dispatches the task to a matching pattern-specific executor: predefined, sequential, hierarchical, or search. A verifier checks whether execution preserves the declared plan structure.

papers.title: Dr. OPD: Learning What to Follow for Optimal On-Policy Distillation of Large Language Models
papers.abstract: This paper introduces Dr. OPD, an improved on-policy distillation method for LLMs. Instead of treating all teacher signals equally, Dr. OPD learns to optimally weight these signals to maximize the student model's performance. This is achieved through a bilevel optimization approach that iteratively updates both the student policy and the signal weights.
papers.figure_caption: Illustration of Dr. OPD. Left: vanilla OPD assigns the same weight to every teacher signal, while Dr. OPD adapts the weights according to their benefit to the student. Right: student rollouts receive teacher and outcome-reward signals, whose gradient alignment determines token credits. These credits are converted into weights for distillation, where \( \lambda \) controls the weighting strength.

papers.title: Gender bias across LLMs is common and highly heterogenous
papers.abstract: This paper investigates gender bias across ten diverse LLMs using two methods: analyzing phrase attribution and moral judgments. It reveals that gender bias is prevalent and varies significantly across models, with some exhibiting masculine-stereotyped phrase attribution to women and others showing a male-disadvantaging moral judgment asymmetry. The study's contribution lies in its broad, comparative analysis, highlighting the heterogeneity of LLM gender biases and their potential real-world implications.

papers.title: Probability is Not Enough: Exploring and Counting Divergent Tokens for Reasoning Uncertainty Quantification in LLMs
papers.abstract: This paper introduces Divergent Token Confidence (DTC), a novel method for quantifying reasoning uncertainty in LLMs. Instead of relying solely on token probabilities, DTC counts tokens where two models disagree significantly during decoding, using Jensen-Shannon divergence to identify these points. This count of divergent tokens is found to be negatively correlated with answer accuracy, providing a more robust signal of model confidence.
papers.figure_caption: Divergent-token selection and its relationship to path accuracy. (a) A generator produces a reasoning trajectory. (b) A token is selected when the JSD between two models’ next-token distributions exceeds \( \theta \) . (c) Path accuracy decreases as the number of divergent tokens increases under single- and dual-auxiliary probing.

papers.title: Retrieval-Augmented Skill Optimization via Cross-Harness Adaptation
papers.abstract: This paper introduces Retrieval-Augmented Skill Optimization (RASO), a method to improve agent skills by leveraging existing knowledge. RASO addresses the inefficiency of current methods by retrieving relevant skills from a large corpus and adapting them to new tasks and environments using Cross-Harness Adaptation. This approach significantly reduces reliance on costly agent simulations by incorporating prior learning.
papers.figure_caption: Comparison of RASO to prior skill optimization. Existing skill optimization methods (left) either generate an initial skill from the LLM alone or directly reuse retrieved skills, then refine them mainly from execution feedback. However, retrieved skills often come from mismatched harnesses; on SpreadsheetBench 92.9% originate from a different harness (right, top). RASO (middle) addresses this by retrieving relevant external skill knowledge and adapting it to the target domain and execution harness through Cross-Harness Adaptation , supporting both skill initialization (RASI) and skill update (RASU). Overall, our RASO results in substantially stronger performance than both direct retrieval and retrieval-free optimization methods.

papers.title: Video-RSI: Recursive Self-Improvement of Video Understanding Agents via Harness Evolution
papers.abstract: Video-RSI recursively improves video understanding agents by using their own language models to revise their observation and action harnesses. The agent actively investigates videos to gather evidence for competing failure explanations, grounding revisions in new observations. This cost-aware evolution leads to improved accuracy with reduced processing costs.

papers.title: Which Attention Heads are like the Human Head? Not the Ones that Compute
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the relationship between brain activity and Large Language Model (LLM) attention heads. It finds that heads aligned with human brain signals (EEG) are causally involved in task performance, but their ablation is less disruptive than heads identified by traditional attribution methods. This suggests that brain alignment and computational contribution are distinct, with concept-aligned heads showing more promise for brain-AI correspondence than function-based ones.

papers.title: Explore Broadly, Reason Sharply: Push Small Models toward the Frontier via Sampling
papers.abstract: This paper introduces Parallel Power Tempering (PPT) to improve reasoning in language models without costly retraining. PPT addresses the exploration-exploitation trade-off in existing sampling methods by running multiple model replicas at different "sharpening" levels. This allows for broader exploration of reasoning paths while still focusing on promising solutions, pushing smaller models closer to state-of-the-art performance.
papers.figure_caption: Single-shot accuracy (%) of Parallel Power Tempering. Left: Qwen3-8B across three benchmarks. Right: Qwen3.5-9B on GPQA-Diamond, AIME 24&25 and LiveCodeBench v5 against decoding baselines and the reported scores of frontier models.
